• [Way forward] Fund indigenous neuroscience research with ethical oversight and translational pathways.
• [Conclusion] An algal protein became a tool for brain circuits, underscoring the case for funding curiosity-driven research alongside translational targets.

• First high-energy cosmic neutrinos were reported in 2013; in 2018 one was traced to a blazar, a galaxy whose supermassive black hole fires a jet almost directly towards Earth.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Nobel Committee for Physics chair Mark Pearce said the instrument paved the way for a new kind of astronomy built on cosmic neutrinos.
• [Issue] Neutrinos are extremely elusive; high-energy ones from violent cosmic collisions are rare, so enormous detector volume is needed to catch enough interactions.
• [Way forward] IceCube will keep revealing violent settings where high-energy neutrinos form and may expose unknown cosmic phenomena; sustained funding for curiosity-led, international big science is the lesson for India.

CA Topic / Headline: SPIR 2026 (Common Cause and Lokniti-CSDS; 8,306 respondents, 16 States/UTs) finds 13% were cybercrime victims in 2-3 years, 54% of them in digital financial fraud; frequent UPI users and the most trusting are likelier victims; victims report banks evade liability.

• 13% of respondents were victims of cybercrime in 2-3 years; 54% of victims faced digital financial fraud; 52% of these complained to the bank separately, 63% of them within 24 hours.
• A 2017 RBI guideline makes the bank fully liable for third-party breaches reported within three days; a 2026 pilot extends limited bank liability to scam payments where customers were tricked or coerced.
• 49% use UPI apps daily; 34% call UPI very safe; fraud kits of pre-activated SIMs, bank accounts and phones sell for ₹10,000-20,000.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Trust paradox: among the highly vulnerable 49% called online banking very safe versus about a fifth of others; victims were likelier to call it very safe (28% against 14%).

CA Topic / Headline: OpenAI to add invisible textGrain watermark to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act, applicable since August 2, 2026; detector flags about 80% of 200-token and 95% of 400-token passages at 1% false-positive rate.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires generative AI providers to mark AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format; the law does not specifically require a watermark.
• OpenAI's textGrain adds a statistical signal to the model's choice of words; from October 5 API customers worldwide can opt for text watermarking on select models.
• Detection: about 80% of 200-token and 95% of 400-token psychology-related passages at a 1% false-positive target; lower for mathematics; editing weakens the signal.
• The European Commission developed a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated content; the detector is initially limited to approved researchers.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Watermarks help counter deepfakes and misinformation but remain provenance signals, not definitive authorship tests, and can be removed by editing.
• [Issue] Detection varies by domain (weak in mathematics), risks false positives and raises privacy questions; OpenAI says the detector will not identify users or reveal prompts.
• [Way forward] Interoperable standards, labelling mandates and detection tools, with safeguards for privacy and due process; India can learn from EU risk-based regulation.

CA Topic / Headline: Editorial 'Break the chain': India must cut leprosy transmission; prevalence under 1 case per 10,000 by 2005 led WHO to declare elimination as a public health problem, but complacency and surveillance folded into general health system let transmission continue; over 70 crore screened in 2025-26.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• WHO declared India to have 'eliminated leprosy as a public health problem' in 2005, when national prevalence fell under 1 case per 10,000 people.
• Targets are set under the National Strategic Plan (NSP) and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027.
• In 2025-26, workers screened over 70 crore people in highly endemic areas, detected 24,367 cases; ASHA workers flagged nearly 40 lakh suspected cases, of which 48,027 were confirmed.
• Single-dose rifampicin was given as post-exposure prophylaxis to 91.1% of the 16.9 lakh likely contacts; digital surveillance is operational and use of the MIP vaccine is under deliberation.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Elimination as a public health problem (a prevalence threshold) is not interruption of transmission; falling registered prevalence hid continuing spread and rising disability from the early 2010s.
• [Issue] Folding vertical surveillance into general health services, shorter registration under multi-drug treatment, stigma-delayed care and clinicians' unfamiliarity or misdiagnosis.
• [Way forward] Prioritise active case finding, contact tracing with post-exposure prophylaxis, digital surveillance, vaccine research and stigma reduction with disability care.

• [Issue] Hundreds of experimental foundries, accessible national labs, flexible compliance and faster approvals for biological materials and clinical trials.
• [Counterpoint] Trust in the research system is low partly because compliance is poor, so deregulation must go with accountability.
• [Way forward] Scale up AI-aided learning, open lab infrastructure to universities and industry and streamline regulation.

CA Topic / Headline: U.S. blockade and decades-old embargo on Cuba: Coast Guard interception of fuel ships worsened power cuts beyond 12 hours a day; Venezuela's lifeline ended after U.S. took control of its oil sector in January 2026; Cuba installs 1,418 MW Chinese-backed solar in 144 parks.

• Cuba installed 1,418 MW of solar capacity in 144 parks (President Diaz-Canel, September 23) and will pass 1,500 MW by end of 2026.

• [Issue] Latin America becomes a venue for US-China-Russia rivalry; China's solar help and trade ties offer Cuba a partial hedge.
• [Counterpoint] Non-binding UNGA votes cannot end an embargo; Cuba's grid, battery storage and reform pace restrict recovery.
• [Issue] India voted with the UNGA majority against the embargo; a sanctions-compliance approach is needed for trade.

CA Topic / Headline: NASA wants a nuclear reactor near the moon's south pole by 2030, planned output 20 kW; Russia's reactor for China-led International Lunar Research Station will produce around 10 kW; Outer Space Treaty 1967 bars appropriation, but temporary safety zones could be used to limit access.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• NASA targets a 20-kW lunar fission reactor near the south pole by 2030; a 20-kW reactor could power a few households on earth.
• Russia's reactor for the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), led by China, will produce around 10 kW.
• The Outer Space Treaty 1967 says no country may claim sovereignty over the moon; the Artemis Accords allow temporary safety zones.
• Research commissioned by NASA recommends situating reactors at least 1 km away from humans; the south pole offers long periods of sunlight and craters with water ice.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] A reactor gives a country controlling advantage over scarce lunar sites despite free-access norms, so safety zones can become de facto claims.
• [Issue] Shielding, heat rejection, dust and launching an unirradiated core are barriers; water ice electrolysis for rocket propellant needs about 68 kW to make 10 tonnes of oxygen.
• [Issue] Update space law to address resource use, safety zones and nuclear safety; India (Artemis Accords signatory) should shape norms through UN COPUOS.
• [Counterpoint] Reactors can contaminate if they fail; consensus on legal limits is weak.

CA Topic / Headline: What is it: Silk Road, network of land and maritime routes linking Asia, important from the second century BC after Han China expanded west; spread papermaking, Buddhism, Christianity, Manichaeism, Islam; aided by Mongol Empire in 13th-14th centuries; declined as Indian Ocean sea routes became cheaper.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The Silk Road took its name from Chinese silk; the network gained importance from about the second century BC, after China's Han dynasty expanded west to Central Asian states.
• Buddhism travelled from India through Central Asia into China; papermaking spread from China along it.
• The Mongol Empire brought much of Eurasia into a connected system in the 13th and 14th centuries.
• Its importance declined by the early modern period as sea trade in the Indian Ocean became cheaper.

• [Issue] Overland trade carried ideas and religions as much as goods; Gandhara art shows Central Asian and Greco-Bactrian influences.

CA Topic / Headline: RBI's Monetary Policy Committee raises the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% and shifts stance from neutral to calibrated tightening; SDF rate 5.25%, MSF and bank rate 5.75%; West Asia re-escalation and crude volatility cited; FY27 GDP forecast raised to 7.1%.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Repo rate raised by 25 bps to 5.5%; SDF rate adjusted to 5.25%, MSF rate and bank rate to 5.75% (corridor: SDF below, MSF above the repo).
• Stance changed from neutral to calibrated tightening; Governor: rate cuts are off the table in the near term, so policy action ahead can only be a hike or a pause.
• Repo was cut to 5.25% in December 2025, held for the next four MPC meetings; the easing cycle had cut 125 bps from 6.5%.
• RBI projections: FY27 GDP growth 7.1% (up from 6.7%); headline CPI to average almost 5.8% over the next three quarters; core inflation 4.4% this financial year.
• Q2 inflation came in at 4.9% against 4.7% projected; RBI sees inflation at 6% (upper tolerance band) in Q3 and 5.7% in Q4.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Hike follows a 125 bps easing cycle; Q2 CPI 4.9% vs 4.7% projected, with fuel and food the main drivers; FPIs sold about $24.3 billion in 2026 against $11.8 billion in 2025.
• [Issue] Inflation is supply-driven (fuel, El Niño-hit food); rates cannot fix supply but curb demand and second-round effects, and the MPC itself says the two are hard to separate.
• [Counterpoint] Hike risks growth and credit cost; analysts note the heavy lifting on inflation falls on the government through fuel and food supply management.
• [Way forward] Pair rate action with buffer stocks, supply-side relief and calibrated fuel pricing; keep policy data-dependent on underlying inflation and second-round effects.
• [Conclusion] Pre-emptive tightening anchors expectations and supports the rupee, but durable disinflation depends on easing energy and food supply constraints.

CA Topic / Headline: RBI to enable interoperability among NBFC account aggregators by December 31, 2026 so people see all financial assets on one platform; SEBI-regulated depositories to add bank deposits to consolidated account statements; data now fragmented across about 15 AAs.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Account Aggregators are RBI-regulated NBFCs offering consent-based sharing of financial data; they route data and do not store it.
• Financial Information Providers (banks, mutual funds, insurers) supply data; Financial Information Users (lenders, wealth managers, insurers) consume it; the AA sits between them.
• Interoperability framework due by December 31, 2026; with customer consent, insurance brokers, asset managers and investment advisers can also access the data.
• Consolidated account statements (CAS) currently exclude bank deposits; inclusion starts with banks already onboarded, others over time; aids tracking of dormant deposits after a holder's death.
• Licensed AAs cited: CAMS FinServ (subsidiary of CAMS) and OneMoney (FinSec AA Solutions).
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Information on assets is split across about 15 AAs; interoperability gives one integrated view, with bank deposits added to CAS.
• [Issue] Fragmented data limits advice and credit assessment; omitted deposits leave the consolidated picture incomplete and dormant deposits unclaimed.
• [Counterpoint] More users on the data rails raise consent-fatigue, mis-selling and cyber-security risks; safeguards must keep pace with access.
• [Way forward] Strong consent architecture aligned with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, grievance redress and audit trails across FIPs, AAs and FIUs.
• [Conclusion] Interoperable AAs can turn consent-based data sharing into a public good, but trust in the consent architecture decides adoption.

CA Topic / Headline: Failure to finalise the India-US trade deal could have some negative impact, says RBI Governor, but new FTAs and export diversification would cushion tariffs; op-ed: the US surplus offsets a structural deficit with China, so a tariff or AI-led export loss would pressure the rupee.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• India follows a managed float: RBI releases dollars to keep a depreciating rupee in its preferred range and adds to reserves when it appreciates beyond it.
• Dollar demand comes from imports and capital outflows (outward FDI + FPI); supply from exports, inward FDI/FPI, transfers, NFIA, external borrowing and deposits.
• FPIs sold about $24.3 billion in Indian markets in 2026 so far against $11.8 billion in 2025.
• RBI: individuals' personal forex transactions fall outside the new FEMA reporting; small exporters with bills up to ₹10 lakh can use self-declaration and an invoice.
• Dollar demand has outpaced supply in four of the last nine quarters (op-ed); India has a structural deficit with China and a surplus with the US, larger in goods than services.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Rising crude after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz plus a possible US tariff would shift the dollar supply curve left and force heavy reserve use.
• [Counterpoint] Governor: effect is premature to judge since sectors and extent are unknown; recent trade agreements and diversified markets mitigate any shock.
• [Way forward] Widen the export product mix and diversify regionally towards the Global South, backed by trade and industrial policy.
• [Conclusion] Treat the tariff threat as a wake-up call: reduce dependence on one market so the surplus is not the only buffer against a structural China deficit.

CA Topic / Headline: Karnataka tells the Supreme Court it may seek reopening of the Cauvery tribunal award on grounds of inequitable allocation and changed circumstances, citing the Centre's own bid to modify the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty; award apportions 740 tmc ft at 50% dependability.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Tribunal award with the Supreme Court's 2018 judgment: 740 tmc ft at 50% dependability at Lower Coleroon Anicut.
• Shares: Karnataka 284.75, Tamil Nadu 404.25, Keralam 30, Puducherry 7 tmc ft; 10 tmc ft for environmental flows and 4 tmc ft inevitable wastage into the sea.
• In a distress year the States share the shortfall pro rata; Karnataka says there is no scientific formula for it.
• Karnataka's 2026 southwest monsoon: 551 mm against 852 mm normal (35% shortfall), second lowest in 70 years after 1956.
• Article 262 lets Parliament adjudicate inter-State river disputes; Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 provides for tribunals. Indus Waters Treaty (1960) is in abeyance.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Karnataka invokes changed circumstances to unravel a decades-old judicial consensus; Tamil Nadu complains of a backlog in releases.
• [Judgment] Award read with the 2018 Supreme Court judgment fixed allocations; Karnataka argues the norms follow a rigid pattern and says allocations are normally revisited periodically.
• [Counterpoint] Reopening settled awards erodes finality and cooperative federalism; the Union's own plea on the Indus treaty muddies the position.
• [Way forward] Notified distress-sharing formula, shared basin data and a standing review mechanism instead of repeated litigation.
• [Conclusion] Cauvery shows a binding award needs a living, data-driven sharing mechanism more than repeated litigation.

CA Topic / Headline: Supreme Court agrees to examine a plea to recall the September 23 split verdict on the CEC and other Election Commissioners Act, 2023; plea questions Justice Satish Chandra Sharma's non-disclosure that his son is an ECI standing counsel.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The 2023 Act replaced the CJI in the PM-led selection panel for CEC and ECs with a Union Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.
• Anoop Baranwal case: a Constitution Bench had included the CJI as a neutral member of the panel until Parliament legislated.
• On September 23 Justice Dipankar Datta declined a five-judge reference while Justice Sharma favoured it; both passed a common order for the CJI to allocate a Constitution Bench.
• Datta J observed the 2023 law was prima facie wrong to ignore Baranwal.
• Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission; Article 324(2) makes appointments subject to a law of Parliament.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Non-disclosure of a family link between a judge and a litigant body raises bias, recusal and public-confidence questions.
• [Judgment] Baranwal's neutral-selector logic versus the 2023 law's executive-heavy panel; the recall plea targets the common order, not Datta J's opinion.
• [Counterpoint] Parliament's power under Article 324(2) and legislative competence versus judicially evolved safeguards for institutional independence.
• [Way forward] Codify disclosure and recusal norms for the bench and restore a balanced, independent selection panel.
• [Conclusion] Election Commission independence rests on a neutral appointment process and on a visibly impartial bench deciding challenges to it.

CA Topic / Headline: Delhi Police detain Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other INDIA bloc leaders for a second day while heading to Jantar Mantar; Opposition vows protests until CEC Gyanesh Kumar resigns; FIR over Akashvani Bhavan entry; police cite 1,000-capacity site, 10-day advance application and prohibitory orders.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Jantar Mantar is a designated protest site with a stated capacity of up to 1,000 people; organisers must approach the concerned DCP office 10 days in advance, and a mere intimation letter is not an application.
• Police have ordered monitoring and, if necessary, pre-emptive detention of past agitators under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
• Facial Recognition System to monitor over 2,800 individuals with criminal antecedents flagged during the July protests; prohibitory orders in force in parts of central Delhi.
• Delhi High Court asked the Centre to consider SOPs for always-on body-worn cameras for police and Rapid Action Force in crowd control; decision within six months.
• Article 19(1)(b): right to assemble peaceably and without arms, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(3).
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Repeated denials of permission, prohibitory orders and pre-emptive detentions of MPs test the right to protest and the Opposition's role in a democracy.
• [Counterpoint] Police cite open calls, uncertain crowd size, last-minute requests, traffic and counter-protest risks; public order is a valid ground for restriction.
• [Way forward] Transparent, time-bound permission criteria with written reasons; body-camera SOPs with storage and retention rules; proportionate use of force and designated alternative sites.
• [Conclusion] The line between maintaining order and curbing dissent is tested by proportionality, reasoned orders and accountable policing.

CA Topic / Headline: West Bengal CEO to hold special camps so voters deleted as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate (ASDD) can return via Form 6; 58 lakh names were left out of the draft roll; tribunals have cleared 1.26 lakh of 38.31 lakh SIR appeals.

• ASDD stands for absent, shifted, dead or duplicate; deleted voters can seek restoration through Form 6; Bengal's Additional CEO says no new voter needs mapping to the 2002 list.
• ECI directed on October 2 that CEOs compare pre-SIR lists with current ones and enrol left-out voters within one month.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):

CA Topic / Headline: Madurai Bench of Madras High Court says organisations engaged in religious conversion shall be denied FCRA registration, dismissing Kanzeon Public Charitable Trust's appeal; a religious organisation with a definite programme can apply but must disclose its nature in Form FC-3A.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Rule 9 of FCRA Rules, 2011: application in Form FC-3A, which requires disclosure of the nature of the organisation.
• Sections 11 and 12 of FCRA: a religious organisation with a definite religious programme may apply for registration; Section 12 bars only an unregistered religious organisation from accepting foreign contributions.
• Bench of Justices G.R. Swaminathan and M.D. Sumathi; the trust, founded by a Christian priest, runs a Zen Meditation Centre at Kodaikanal.
• Application rejected because the trust did not correctly identify itself as religious; Zen Buddhism is a variant of the Mahayana school.
• Court quoted the salad-bowl metaphor for pluralism, credited to Justice Ruma Pal, in contrast to the American melting pot.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Foreign funding to religious bodies versus the Centre's policy to check inflows used for conversion that harm the secular fabric.
• [Judgment] Court: only organisations whose activities do not affect the nation's secular fabric and social amity are entitled to registration; concealment of nature is fatal.
• [Counterpoint] Article 25 freedom of religion and association rights; vague tests of conversion risk arbitrary denial and chilling of charity.
• [Way forward] Objective, published criteria for registration and renewal, reasoned orders and an appeal route, with transparency on foreign inflows.
• [Conclusion] Regulating foreign funding is legitimate, but published standards and reasoned orders keep it from curbing religious freedom.

CA Topic / Headline: Arunachal Christian Forum alleges SBI's digital banking software disables the Scheduled Tribe option for applicants who choose Christianity, auto-classifying them as general; forum warns of agitation if not corrected within 15 days; SBI says it is looking into the matter.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Forum cites the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950: tribal status in Arunachal Pradesh is not contingent on religion.
• Article 342: the President specifies Scheduled Tribes, by public notification, State by State; Parliament may modify the list by law.
• Letter to SBI's Itanagar regional manager, received October 5, sets a 15-day deadline; ACF president James Techi Tara and secretary general Yomrik Lombi signed it.
• ACF asks SBI to clarify whether any RBI directive permits such classification and to stop treating religion and tribal status as mutually exclusive.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Software logic that equates a declared religion with social category denies tribal Christians their ST identity in KYC and account opening.
• [Counterpoint] ST status flows from the Constitution and the ST certificate, not faith; the bank is not the competent authority to de-list a tribal.
• [Way forward] Audit on-boarding logic, align KYC fields with the ST Order and certificate, and add grievance redress and RBI oversight of algorithmic classification.
• [Conclusion] Technology must implement constitutional categories, not rewrite them; algorithmic KYC needs the same equality scrutiny as public rules.

CA Topic / Headline: Henri Kagan (France) and Kenso Soai (Japan) win the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing how chemical reactions can amplify small asymmetries in chiral molecules; Kagan's 1986 catalyst work and Soai's reaction in which a chiral molecule speeds formation of its own handedness.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• 2026 Chemistry Nobel: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, for work on amplifying small asymmetries in chiral (mirror-image) molecules.
• Chiral molecules exist in two mirror-image forms, like left and right hands; proteins are made mostly of one handedness of amino acids.
• Kagan (1986): a small imbalance in a catalyst's handedness can disproportionately bias the reaction's products; Soai: a chiral molecule can speed formation of molecules with its own handedness.
• Relevance: tuning reactions to produce the desired form of a drug, agrochemical or fragrance.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Differently handed forms of a drug interact differently with chiral enzymes and receptors, so only one form may be therapeutic.
• [Issue] Making only the desirable form was a manufacturing challenge; asymmetric amplification and catalysis reduce waste and cost.
• [Way forward] Invest in green and asymmetric catalysis for India's pharma and agrochemical sectors to move up the value chain.
• [Conclusion] Chirality explains why molecular handedness matters in medicines; asymmetric catalysis is a strategic capability for pharma-exporting economies.

Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• IceCube: neutrino detector under Antarctic ice; sensors up to 2.5 km beneath the South Pole record light flashes when neutrinos interact with ice atoms.
• Operational since 2011; detects high-energy neutrinos from astronomical sources, strengthening neutrino astronomy.
• Collaboration of over 400 experts from 14 countries; Nobel statutes bar dividing a prize among more than three individuals.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Nobel statutes allow prizes to organisations but this is repeatedly overlooked, entrenching a distorted, individual-genius view of science.
• [Counterpoint] Prestige and tradition make rule changes slow; committees say identifying leadership is practical.
• [Way forward] Recognise collaborations and teams in awards and funding, including India's own big-science projects.
• [Conclusion] Modern science is collective, so recognition and funding should reward teams, institutions and instrument builders.

CA Topic / Headline: Cement, a hard-to-abate sector, emits 7-11% of global emissions; NITI Aayog roadmap seeks 20% thermal substitution by refuse-derived fuel by 2030 and lower clinker ratio (India 67.5% vs global 77%); production to rise from 334 million tonnes (2019-20) to 1,546 million tonnes by 2070.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Calcination of limestone releases CO2 and clinker; kiln heating to about 1,450°C accounts for 35-40% of emissions, clinker for 53-65%.
• Ordinary Portland cement has over 95% clinker; Portland pozzolana cement 65-80%; Portland slag cement 35-64%.
• NITI Aayog roadmap: raise RDF use from municipal solid waste to 20% thermal substitution by 2030, a cumulative cut of about 80 million tonnes CO2-equivalent.
• IEA: replacing one tonne of clinker avoids 0.83 tonnes of CO2; TERI: target 0.56 tCO2 per tonne of cement by 2030 and 0.51 by 2047, from 0.62.
• Average clinker substitution cannot exceed about 40% in practice even though options go to 50-70%; India's clinker-to-cement ratio is 67.5% against 77% globally.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Electoral Rolls, ECI & Judiciary
CA Topic / Headline: Op-ed: SIR struck 13.37 crore names off draft rolls across 30 States and UTs, deletion rates rising from 8.3% in Bihar to 17% in Phase 3; flaws cited include inverted enumeration, Form 6 re-entry, logical-discrepancy software, ERONet centralisation and a deferential Supreme Court.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• 13.37 crore names struck off at draft stage in three SIR phases across 30 States and UTs: 65 lakh in Bihar, 6.57 crore in Phase 2 (12 States/UTs) and 6.15 crore in Phase 3, whose final rolls are yet to be published.
• Deletion rate rose from 8.3% (Bihar) to 12.9% (Phase 2) and 17% (Phase 3), with 32.8% in Delhi and 21.7% in Telangana; Delhi's draft roll has 97.54 lakh electors against 94.95 lakh who voted in February 2025, and 24 of 70 constituencies show fewer electors than voters.
• Section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 allows a special revision "for any constituency or part of a constituency"; the Court allowed its use State-wide, outside the Registration of Electors Rules.
• Lal Babu Hussein (1995): three-judge Bench struck down a sweeping revision demanding citizenship documents from nearly 18,000 residents of Matia Mahal, Delhi; a name on the roll is presumed valid and removable only after notice and hearing.
• Form 6 (new voters) must also be used by deleted voters seeking re-entry, so returning and new voters cannot be separated; ERONet database changes override Electoral Registration Officers, the statutory authorities on eligibility.
• West Bengal: 60 lakh flagged for logical discrepancies, judicial officers struck off 27 lakh; tribunals restored 93% of decided cases (about one lakh names) but disposed only 1.22 lakh of over 38 lakh appeals (3.2%) by early September.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] ECI's Manual on Electoral Rolls (2023) treats an intensive revision as a fresh enumeration by visiting every house (paragraph 9.3.1) and gives probative value to presence on the earlier roll (paragraph 7.4.2); SIR instead puts the onus on electors.
• [Issue] Exclusion by design: software flagged spelling mismatches, more than six voters per ancestor and parent-child age gaps outside 15 to 45 years; Bihar's gender ratio in final SIR rolls fell to 892 from 907 in the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls; SABAR Institute estimated 65% of West Bengal deletions were Muslims against about 27% of the population.
• [Judgment] The Court asked only whether SIR was "manifestly excessive", not whether a less harmful method existed, and sidestepped Lal Babu Hussein (1995); the author seeks review or a Constitution Bench.
• [Issue] Dissent within the ECI: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded at least 14 objections between October 2025 and August 2026, including Form 6 being altered without amending the rules.
• [Way forward] Halt SIR, audit rolls finalised so far, return to door-to-door verification by Booth Level Officers, and let poll-bound States use pre-SIR rolls updated with fresh enrolments.
• [Counterpoint] ECI says SIR purifies the rolls of ineligible entries and has ordered a special drive to enrol anyone left out; accurate rolls are an electoral integrity requirement too.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Preventive Detention & Fundamental Rights
CA Topic / Headline: Allahabad High Court questions use of the term andolanjeevi in an NSA detention order by the Gautam Buddha Nagar DM against journalist Satyam Verma, an accused in the Noida workers' protests; asks how ideology or reading material can justify preventive detention; order reserved.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Detention order of May 12 by Gautam Buddha Nagar District Magistrate Medha Roopam under the National Security Act against journalist Satyam Verma; Justice Atul Sreedharan's Bench reserved its order on his plea seeking quashing, release and compensation.
• The order, in Hindi, called him an illogical, stubborn and violent andolanjeevi with a warped ideology; the term was popularised by the PM in a Rajya Sabha speech on February 8, 2021 on the 2020-21 farmers' agitation.

• [Counterpoint] Preventive detention exists to forestall violence; the State alleges Verma indirectly incited industrial workers to commit violence, arson and vandalism.

GS Area: GS3 Internal Security – Social Media, Deepfakes & IT Rules

• Advisory asks platforms to curb manipulated or out-of-context content, over and above AI-generated deepfakes already liable for takedown notices under amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Liability and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021; first reported by MediaNama.
• The advisory says such content, when presented as authentic, can cause public confusion, disturb public order and contribute to law-and-order concerns.

• [Issue] Official social media campaigns by police to counter what they call cyber warfare blur public information with narrative management during a live protest.
• [Way forward] Narrow, defined categories, due-process takedowns with reasons and appeal, platform transparency reports, media-literacy drives and techno-legal tools for provenance of AI content.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] A new statute governing cadres of the Union's paramilitary forces is in force while its validity and the SC's 2025 cadre judgment are both before the Court.

• [Issue] Institutional angle: CAPFs are manned by the Union but operate with State police, so command structures link the All India Services, MHA and State governments.
• [Counterpoint] IPS leadership gives CAPFs coordination with State police and civil administration in internal-security duties, so a sudden cut can affect operational command.
• [Way forward] Phase deputation against a published time-bound cadre review, protect career progression for CAPF cadre officers, and let the Court examine the Act on merits instead of through contempt alone.

Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Stubble burning is concentrated from October to November in Punjab, Haryana and parts of UP; the two States produce around 29 million metric tons of paddy straw.
• Punjab Preservation of Sub-Soil Water Act (PPSSWA), 2009 bars sowing paddy before May 10 and transplanting before June 10, with a penalty of ₹10,000 per hectare for every month of contravention; it pushed harvest to late October and left a 10-15-day window before wheat sowing.
• Between 2012 and 2024 average paddy procurement was about 37% of production nationally against 87% in Punjab and 74% in Haryana; for wheat it was 30% nationally, 70% in Punjab and 63% in Haryana.
• In-situ solutions: Happy Seeders, Super Seeders, Rotavators, short-duration rice varieties, direct seeding of rice; ex-situ: crop residue for bio-ethanol and compressed biogas (CBG). A Happy Seeder needs a 60-HP tractor, with hire costing about ₹10,000; ex-situ measures cost ₹1,500-₹2,500 per acre.
• Haryana incentives: ₹1,000 per acre for CRM use, ₹4,000 per acre for direct seeding of rice, ₹7,000 per acre for diversification; the NGT ruled in 2018 that farmers who burn stubble could be excluded from MSP, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2023.
• CREAMS protocol relies on NASA's MODIS and VIIRS polar satellites, which observe India only between 10:30 am and 1:30 pm; an ISRO-led Current Science study (November 2025) found farmers shifted burning to evening hours, and suggests adding geostationary data.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Punjab and Haryana reported about a 90% reduction in burning incidents in 2025 vs 2022 (Lok Sabha reply of December 1, 2025), but multi-satellite data suggests a fall closer to 30%.
• [Issue] The problem is rooted in incentives: assured procurement of paddy and wheat plus free power sustain water-intensive crops despite groundwater depletion; PPSSWA 2009 solved water use but shifted burning into winter.
• [Issue] Technology and cost gaps: machines are expensive and shared poorly, ex-situ demand for residue is weak, and measurement hides evening burning.
• [Counterpoint] Punitive tools (MSP exclusion, penalties on officials) may encourage collusion between farmers and officials to 'show' a reduction; the Parliamentary Committee wants penalising farmers as a last resort.
• [Way forward] Crop diversification with assured procurement of alternatives, a minimum price for residue for ex-situ users, better CRM machine access, and measurement using both polar and geostationary satellites.

GS Area: GS2 Polity & GS1 Society – Article 17, Caste, Atrocities
CA Topic / Headline: Parley: are legal guarantees insufficient in ending untouchability? Valerian Rodrigues and Disha Wadekar on Article 17, criminal law's limits, civil remedies and 'reactionary atrocities'; context is a ritual to 'cleanse' an area after Mallikarjun Kharge's rally, defended by the Uttarakhand BJP chief.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Article 17 (Part III, Right to Equality) abolishes 'untouchability' and forbids its practice in any form; enforcement of any disability arising out of it is an offence punishable by law.
• Parliament enacted the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 in 1976; the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 covers caste-based atrocities.
• Article 17 operates against private individuals as well as the State, so it is a right enforceable horizontally.
• Trigger: Uttarakhand BJP chief defended a ritual that was meant to 'cleanse' the area of the ideas that Mr. Kharge, who belongs to a Dalit community, had espoused at a rally; an FIR was registered after a sustained campaign by Opposition leaders and civil society.
• Rodrigues: legal guarantees are necessary but not adequate; he points to Ambedkar's view that untouchable practices must be abolished and Gandhi's view that social conscience must change; Wadekar suggests civil remedies, with a lower burden of proof, as used in the POSH Act, and localised dispute resolution through Gram Sabhas.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Article 17 and two central laws exist since 1950-1989, yet 'reactionary' forms of atrocity target Dalit mobility, as in the Reservation Hatao Andolan; Ambedkar called untouchability a 'notion in the mind'.
• [Issue] Criminal law carries deterrence value but a proof 'beyond reasonable doubt' threshold; it will not end atrocities by itself.
• [Issue] Civil remedies: lower burden of proof and civil punishments, as the POSH Act does for gender discrimination, have not been explored for caste discrimination.
• [Counterpoint] Reluctance to criminalise everything is valid: due-process safeguards and community-level dispute resolution have to be balanced against victim protection.
• [Way forward] A civil anti-discrimination law, Gram Sabha forums, speedy trials, reservation in local governance and social reform movements working beside legal reform.

GS Area: GS3 Economy – FDI, Ease of Doing Business, Trade Agreements
CA Topic / Headline: Op-ed (Bharat Joshi): Calibrating India's inbound investment framework — record gross FDI of $94.8 billion in FY26, 11th among top FDI destinations (UNCTAD WIR 2026); bottlenecks: Centre-State coordination, labour codes rollout, QCOs (about 790), nearly 48 million pending court cases.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Reserve Bank of India data show gross inward FDI reached a record $94.8 billion in FY26; UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026 ranks India 11th among the top FDI destinations after a 44% rise in inflows.
• India received about $7 billion in greenfield data-centre investments in the first three quarters of 2025, behind South Korea ($21 billion), the US ($29 billion) and France ($69 billion).
• Labour codes: 29 central labour laws were consolidated into four codes; Central Rules were notified in May 2026, but labour is on the Concurrent List so implementation depends on State notifications (Gujarat notified rules under all four).
• Gauba Committee found Quality Control Orders (QCOs) grew from fewer than 70 to nearly 790; imported-component compliance costs rose to ₹20 lakh with six- to eight-month certification; QCOs on PVC, aluminium and zinc were withdrawn.
• India-EFTA TEPA sets a $100-billion investment target but lacks an independent bilateral investment dispute mechanism; DPIIT's revised SOP (May 2026) sets a 12-week deadline; Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 ended retrospective tax disputes (Vodafone, Cairn).
• Mobile-phone production grew 33-fold since FY15 from ₹180 billion to ₹6.27 trillion; India is the second-largest mobile-phone manufacturer and meets 99.2% of domestic demand.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Record FDI and an 11th rank globally, yet global international project finance is about a quarter below its 2021 peak and the lag between committed and deployed greenfield capital persists.
• [Issue] Many remaining reforms are internal: Centre-State, DPIIT-Ministry and central-rule-State-notification gaps, as seen in labour codes.
• [Issue] Compliance and dispute resolution: QCO expansion, 48 million pending court cases (about six million in High Courts), and no bilateral investment dispute mechanism in the India-EFTA TEPA.
• [Counterpoint] Quality Control Orders protect consumers and domestic manufacturing, while relaxing them may allow dumping; FDI headline numbers include equity reinvestment and transfers, not only fresh capex.
• [Way forward] Single-window clearance with deadlines, a Centre-State coordination mechanism, faster commercial benches and mediation, and investor-protection clauses in FTAs and BITs.

CA Topic / Headline: Govt caps trade margins at 30% of MRP for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs (NPPA found average mark-up around 170%, up to 700%); Supreme Court directs an expert committee on unethical pharma marketing within two weeks, report in two months, on petitions by FMRAI.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Centre decided to cap trade margins at 30% of maximum retail price (MRP) for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs, covering branded and generic, domestic and imported, patented and non-patented products.
• An expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) will finalise the list of medicines covered; the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) found average trade mark-up on non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs of around 170%, reaching up to 700% in some cases.
• Supreme Court directed the Union government to constitute an expert committee within two weeks to strengthen the regulatory regime against unethical pharmaceutical marketing; it must consult stakeholders and report within two months of its first meeting.
• Petitions were filed by the Federation of Medical and Sales Representatives' Associations of India (FMRAI) and others.
• Static: NPPA functions under the Department of Pharmaceuticals and fixes ceiling prices for scheduled drugs under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013; the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP), 2024 is the existing marketing code.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Trade mark-ups of about 170% on average, up to 700%, make out-of-pocket spending on cancer care a major household burden.

• [Issue] Price control only on the retail margin leaves manufacturer prices uncontrolled for non-scheduled drugs; product list finalisation decides actual impact.
• [Counterpoint] Margin caps can squeeze retailers and chemists, and drugs may be shifted to unregulated formulations; innovation incentives need protection.
• [Way forward] A statutory marketing code with penalties, transparent disclosure of payments to doctors, expanding the National List of Essential Medicines, and generic prescribing by name.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Federalism, CBI & Centre-State Relations
CA Topic / Headline: Supreme Court defers to Friday Punjab's appeal against the High Court order for a CBI probe into corruption allegations linked to CM Mann's office; Mann calls the CBI raid on his camp office a BJP poll campaign; case against OSD Rajbir Ghuman.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• CBI registered a corruption case on Tuesday against Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann's Officer on Special Duty Rajbir Ghuman and five others after the Punjab and Haryana High Court directed it to probe allegations linked to his office.
• Allegations: influencing postings of IAS and IPS officers, departmental proceedings, policy formulation, administrative approvals, tender conditions, licensing, land-use conversion, property disputes and revenue and land issues for pecuniary advantage.
• The Supreme Court on Thursday deferred to Friday the hearing of Punjab's appeal; Justice Dipankar Datta said Justice Sheel Nagu had yet to receive the case file; Punjab sought an interim stay citing federalism and statutory safeguards.
• Mann said the CBI search at the CM's camp office showed the Punjab Assembly election would be held on time and accused the BJP of beginning its poll campaign through investigative agencies; the BJP said it did not order the probe and the court did.
• Static: CBI is governed by the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, which requires State consent (Section 6) for investigation in a State, but constitutional courts can direct a CBI probe without consent.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] The state-vs-CBI contest turns on State consent under the DSPE Act versus the powers of High Courts and the Supreme Court under Articles 226 and 32.
• [Issue] Political timing: ahead of Punjab elections, central agency action invites charges of selective targeting.
• [Counterpoint] Where a High Court finds a prima facie case and doubts State police independence, an independent probe protects the rule of law.
• [Way forward] Statutory autonomy for the CBI, clear criteria for court-directed probes and a Centre-State protocol on agency action.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Fundamental Rights (Art 19), Law & Order
CA Topic / Headline: Delhi Police deny permission for the CJP's 10 October Jantar Mantar protest against the CEC and SIR; MHA asks States to stop movement towards Delhi; 245 trains cancelled, 57 Metro stations shut. SC calls the blanket transit ban over-reaching.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Article 19(1)(b) guarantees citizens the right to assemble peaceably and without arms; Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order.
• Prohibitory orders in New Delhi are under Section 163 of the BNSS, successor to CrPC Section 144; Noida's order bars assemblies of five or more persons from 10 to 20 October.
• Delhi Police set up holding centres in all 15 police districts and over 30 blocking points in New Delhi district; over 50,000 Delhi Police and CAPF personnel, including CISF, SSB and ITBP, were deployed.
• Railways cancelled 245 trains (75 Mail/Express including Rajdhani, Tejas and Shatabdi, and 170 passenger trains) with a 100% refund; police said permission for such events is ordinarily sought at least 10 days in advance.
• SC Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant distinguished total prohibition from regulation of Metro and rail movement; Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta assured the Bench he would press authorities to reassess the travel prohibitions.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Delhi was effectively locked down: internet curbs, closed markets and Metro stations, schools and colleges online, and about 13,000 additional Central personnel (6,000 ITBP/SSB plus 7,000 CRPF) over the Delhi Police.
• [Issue] Proportionality: assembly is a fundamental right, but city-wide pre-emptive restrictions hit commuters, patients and students; senior counsel argued a peaceful protest is not illegal for lack of permission unless an offence occurs.
• [Counterpoint] Police cite non-compliance with undertakings in an earlier protest, short notice (request made 7 October) and intelligence of attempted entry from other States; Justice Bagchi said a protest without permission may prove illegal.
• [Way forward] Designate a spacious, equipped protest site, as the SC suggested (central Delhi lacks washrooms, medical and drinking-water facilities); restrict narrowly and proportionately and publicise decisions widely.

CA Topic / Headline: Delhi Police impose a 24-hour internet shutdown within four km of the Janpath-Kartavya Path intersection from 10 p.m. Friday; IT Ministry advisory asks platforms to limit reach of public-order content and prioritise government takedown requests.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Delhi Police Special Cell notified a 24-hour internet shutdown from 10 p.m. Friday within a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path intersection.
• IT Ministry advisory urges platforms to limit reach of content likely to cause public disorder and to give priority to complaints from authorised government agencies.
• Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 is the statutory blocking power; Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A but upheld Section 69A with safeguards.
• Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020): indefinite internet suspension is impermissible; orders must be published, necessary, proportionate and subject to review.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Shutdowns cut access to news, payments and emergency services for everyone in the zone, not only protesters; the advisory is non-statutory yet pressures intermediaries.
• [Counterpoint] Authorities argue rapid spread of inciting or unverified content can inflame public order, so time-bound, geographically limited suspensions and priority takedowns are preventive tools.
• [Way forward] Publish shutdown orders with reasons, cap duration, ensure independent review on Anuradha Bhasin standards, and give platforms and users notice and appeal against takedowns.

CA Topic / Headline: SC stands by its ban on unauthorised use and circulation of live-streamed court proceedings on social media and digital platforms, saying material meant for public good cannot be exploited commercially; viewing and reporting remain permitted; parties given time to file suggestions.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• SC Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant reaffirmed its bar on unauthorised use and circulation of live-streamed proceedings on social media and digital platforms.
• The bar is not a gag: viewing live-streamed proceedings and court reportage remain permitted; parties and stakeholders were given time to file pleadings and suggestions.
• Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India (2018) permitted live-streaming of constitutional-bench proceedings, anchored in the open-court principle and access to justice.
• Justice Joymalya Bagchi noted proceedings are live-streamed 24x7 in the United Kingdom and the United States, subject to strict guidelines against commercialisation.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Open justice improves transparency and access, but clipping hearings for virality or revenue risks distorting proceedings, harming litigants and pressuring judges.
• [Counterpoint] Blanket limits on circulation may curb legitimate commentary, journalism and legal education; the SC stressed viewing and reporting are unaffected.
• [Way forward] Frame licensed non-commercial reuse rules with penalties for monetised clips, official searchable archives and transcripts, and periodic review of the guidelines.

CA Topic / Headline: Delhi SIR: over 15 lakh of 33.1 lakh notices disposed after new ECINET options let EROs mark electors eligible on a hearing order without documents or hearing; EROs are split on using it; 19.1 lakh are logical-discrepancy cases.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):

• All 33.1 lakh noticed electors are on the draft roll; 19.1 lakh cases are logical discrepancies, flagged by the system and unrelated to eligibility.
• ECI's prescribed list of 12 documents excludes bank passbooks, PAN and Aadhaar; BLOs upload them with their own undertaking after field verification, and were asked to collect documents for at least 10 cases a day.
• Article 326 provides for elections on adult suffrage; Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the ECI.

• [Counterpoint] Field-report-based clearance helps genuine but poorly documented voters, yet without written SOPs practice varies across EROs, weakening uniformity and legal defensibility.
• [Way forward] Issue written, published instructions on hearing orders, set document-light verification standards, audit samples of disposals and provide an appeal route with timelines.

CA Topic / Headline: ECI caps Form 7 deletion objections at 10 per elector during claims and objections and five a month during continuous updation, online and physical; booth-level agents limited to 50 forms a day before draft rolls and 10 after; false complaints invite ERO action.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Form 7 seeks deletion of a name or objection to an entry in the electoral roll; Form 6 seeks inclusion.
• New caps: 10 Form 7s per individual during claims and objections; five a month during continuous updation; applies to online and physical forms (physical Form 7s had no limit earlier).
• Booth-level agents of recognised parties may file at most 50 forms a day before draft publication and 10 a day after.
• Manual on Electoral Rolls, 2023, para 11.3.2(ii): bulk claims and objections by an individual are not entertained; the ERO must personally cross-verify if the same objector appears in more than five cases.
• Under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, a claim or objection not lodged in the specified period, form and manner is rejected by the ERO.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Bulk Form 7 filings can weaponise deletion, burdening objected-upon electors and field staff; The Hindu reported bulk Form 7s filed in the names of BJP leaders from Rajasthan, Gujarat, West Bengal and Karnataka.
• [Counterpoint] Caps may hinder genuine objections by vigilant citizens; limits on party agents must secure transparency without blocking legitimate challenge.
• [Way forward] Verify objectors, publish Form 7 data booth-wise, mandate notice and hearing before deletion, penalise fabricated complaints and maintain audit trails.

CA Topic / Headline: MP HC strikes down the 2019 law raising OBC reservation from 14% to 27%, finding no extraordinary circumstances to breach the 50% ceiling; SC upholds the A.P. HC verdict against 34% BC quota in local bodies, saying family-survey data is not specific empirical proof.

• Indra Sawhney (1992) set the 50% ceiling with exceptions only in extraordinary situations; for local bodies the triple test is a dedicated commission, empirical data on backwardness and the 50% cap (Vikas Kishanrao Gawali, 2021).
• SC Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu dismissed A.P.'s appeal against the 1 October HC verdict that the State lacked empirical data to breach the 50% ceiling for BC quota in local bodies.

• [Counterpoint] OBCs are over 50% of MP's population and States argue population share justifies larger quotas; BJP and Congress blamed each other for the collapse of the State's case.
• [Way forward] Build robust caste and representation data, set up dedicated commissions, apply the triple test for local bodies and seek constitutional clarity on the ceiling rather than ad hoc State laws.

• CRR is the share of net demand and time liabilities that banks hold with the RBI; it earns no interest. The requirement itself is unchanged; the daily maintenance threshold is raised.

• [Issue] Tightening daily maintenance drains surplus liquidity, helps transmission of policy rates and curbs credit-fuelled inflation without changing the headline CRR.

• [Way forward] Combine liquidity tools such as VRRR and OMOs with clear communication, calibrated to inflation and growth data.

• [Judgment] Puttaswamy requires legality, legitimate aim and proportionality for state intrusion on privacy.
• [Way forward] Statutory regulation of FRT, purpose limitation under the Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 and retention schedules, independent oversight and deletion rights.

GS Area: GS2 Social Sector – Health; GS3 Science & Tech
CA Topic / Headline: WHO issues first clinical guidelines on child and adolescent obesity: advises against anti-obesity drugs including GLP-1 agonists and bariatric surgery for ages 0–9; 170 million aged 5–19 with obesity (2024); CDSCO approved semaglutide for adolescents aged 12 and above only for morbid obesity with comorbidities.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• WHO's first guidelines on managing obesity in children and adolescents advise against anti-obesity drugs, including GLP-1 receptor agonists, and bariatric surgery for ages 0–9; family-centred behaviour change is the standard of care.
• For ages 10–19, drugs may be considered only if a supervised multimodal lifestyle programme fails; bariatric surgery only under strict conditions for severe obesity.
• Rationale: lack of long-term trial data on paediatric safety, efficacy and tapering for drugs such as semaglutide.
• Global burden (2024): 170 million aged 5–19 live with obesity (70 million aged 5–9; 100 million aged 10–19); the fastest growth is in low- and middle-income countries.
• India: obese boys rose from 0.2 million (1990) to 7.3 million (2022), girls from 0.2 million to 5.2 million; CNNS projects over 27 million obese youth, 11% of the global burden; CDSCO approved semaglutide for adolescents aged 12 and above.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] India faces a double burden: undernutrition coexists with fast-rising child obesity.
• [Issue] Drug-first approaches lack long-term safety data; surgery risks micronutrient malabsorption and impaired growth in children.
• [Counterpoint] For severe obesity with comorbidities such as NAFLD and prediabetes, regulated drug use may be justified under supervision.
• [Way forward] School-based nutrition and physical-activity programmes, front-of-pack labelling, curbs on marketing of junk food to children and mental-health support against stigma.

CA Topic / Headline: DRDO flight-tests an indigenous High Altitude Platform System (HAPS): reached 21 km above mean sea level and held 20 km for over 30 minutes; developed by ADRDE, Agra; real-time data to Ground Control Station; recovered after commanded descent.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• DRDO's HAPS reached 21 km above mean sea level and held 20 km for over 30 minutes.
• The ITU defines HAPS as stations on platforms at 20–50 km altitude; it bridges the gap between aircraft and satellites.
• Developed by the Aerial Delivery Research and Development Establishment (ADRDE), Agra, a DRDO laboratory; involves the IAF, CEMILAC, DGCA, AAI and other civil authorities.
• Payload and systems: Inertial Measurement Unit, GPS receiver, onboard cameras and an altitude-control mechanism; the platform descended on command and was recovered.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Long-endurance stratospheric platforms can support surveillance, communications, Earth observation and disaster response at lower cost than satellites.
• [Counterpoint] Technology is at an early flight-test stage; endurance, payload, weather resilience and airspace regulation remain unproven.
• [Way forward] Move from tests to long-duration trials, integrate with ISR and 6G non-terrestrial networks, and fund private-sector participation under Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Fundamental Rights; Police Powers
CA Topic / Headline: Thousands are detained to stop a march seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, with Section 163 BNSS in force in New Delhi district; ex-Justice Abhay Oka says Article 22 requires grounds of detention "as soon as may be"; a habeas corpus plea reaches the Supreme Court.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaced Section 144 of the CrPC; an executive magistrate may issue prohibitory orders where immediate prevention or speedy remedy is desirable.
• Article 22 requires the grounds of arrest or detention to be communicated; the National Security Act, 1980 is a preventive detention law under Article 22(3)-(7).
• A habeas corpus petition under Article 32 sought production of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka before a Special Bench of the Supreme Court.
• Over 20,000 security personnel were deployed, 45 Metro stations shut and over 200 trains arriving in Delhi cancelled.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Detaining rather than arresting lets police skip safeguards such as production before a magistrate; the Supreme Court has not conclusively settled how arrest safeguards apply to brief protest detentions.
• [Judgment] Justice Oka says Article 22's protection cannot be circumvented by calling a restraint detention rather than arrest; advocates cite rulings making communication of grounds a sine qua non even under the NSA.
• [Counterpoint] Delhi Police say detentions followed violations of Section 163 orders and that due process would follow for CJP leaders; India says protest rights are subject to reasonable restrictions.
• [Way forward] Publish detention orders with grounds, avoid mass detentions outside areas where orders apply, designate protest sites such as Ramlila Maidan and fix accountability for missing name-tags.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Fundamental Rights; GS3 Internal Security
CA Topic / Headline: Internet is shut in central Delhi, leaving commuters unable to use maps or pay digitally, tourists stranded and autorickshaw drivers without bookings; daily-wage workers lose a day's pay as barricades lock them out; CPI(M) says 57 Metro stations were closed.

• Only people with government ID cards were allowed to proceed towards central Delhi; over 200 trains arriving in Delhi were cancelled.
• Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020) held that indefinite internet suspension is impermissible and that orders must be proportionate and reviewable.
• Temporary suspension of telecom services is regulated under the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and rules made under it.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] An autorickshaw driver lost 30-40 trips at Connaught Place; construction workers, an electrician and gig workers lost the day's pay as barricades blocked central Delhi.
• [Judgment] In Anuradha Bhasin (2020) the Supreme Court read internet access as integral to the freedoms under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), subject to proportionality.
• [Counterpoint] The UN rights office says restrictions must meet the test of necessity and proportionality; the government says reasonable restrictions apply in the interest of public order.
• [Way forward] Publish suspension orders, review them periodically, use targeted rather than blanket shutdowns and provide exemptions for payments and essential services.

CA Topic / Headline: Madhya Pradesh High Court strikes down the 2019 law raising OBC reservation from 14% to 27%, as unconstitutional and breaching the 50% ceiling, with no extraordinary circumstances; Congress will appeal to the Supreme Court and questions the survey's data.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Indra Sawhney (1992) capped total reservation at 50% save in extraordinary circumstances; the High Court held the 2019 law, which lifted the OBC quota from 14% to 27%, breached it.
• Article 16(4) lets the State reserve posts for backward classes inadequately represented in State services; Article 15(4) enables special provisions in education.
• The High Court's 159-page order found no extraordinary circumstances to justify exceeding the 50% ceiling.
• Congress says a survey of just 10,000 people was used to assess a State of about 7.26 crore.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] The 50% ceiling and State-level data on backwardness collide with demands for proportional representation; courts require contemporaneous, quantifiable data to justify exceeding it.
• [Judgment] In Jaishri Patil (2021) the Supreme Court declined to revisit the 50% cap and held that States must show extraordinary circumstances, not merely inadequate representation.
• [Counterpoint] Congress alleges the BJP government failed to defend the quota with adequate data; the government spent heavily on legal proceedings but did not secure a favourable outcome.
• [Way forward] Collect caste-wise quantifiable data through a dedicated commission, then seek judicial review or a constitutional amendment with Ninth Schedule safeguards tested under the basic structure.

Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); the Second Judges Case (1993) gave primacy to the CJI in appointments.
• The 99th Constitutional Amendment and the NJAC Act, 2014 were struck down in 2015 in the Fourth Judges Case.

Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] If the executive controls the pace of clearing names, collegium primacy becomes nominal, undermining judicial independence and the separation of powers.
• [Judgment] The Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in 2015 as violating the basic structure, but conceded that the collegium needs greater transparency.
• [Counterpoint] Defenders of executive participation argue judge-only appointments are opaque and unaccountable, and that elected institutions must have a role in selecting constitutional functionaries.
• [Way forward] Publish collegium reasons, set time limits for the government to clear names, review the Memorandum of Procedure and create a permanent secretariat.

CA Topic / Headline: Two Nature papers from Europe and China report the world's first working nuclear clocks using thorium-229, whose nucleus can be excited by an ultraviolet laser; the Austria-Germany clock, run beside a ytterbium atomic clock to search for dark matter, finds no signal.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Thorium-229 has a nuclear transition energy low enough to be triggered by an ultraviolet laser, unlike most nuclei that need X-rays or gamma rays.
• The Beijing-Shanghai team embedded thorium-229 in calcium fluoride crystals; the Austria-Germany team used its clock to look for dark matter.
• A ytterbium atomic clock is so precise it misses one second every 23 billion years.
• The nucleus is shielded by the electron cloud, so a nuclear clock is less disturbed by electric or magnetic fields and temperature changes than an atomic clock.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Atomic clocks are the gold standard behind GPS navigation and synchronised networks; scientists want greater precision to detect tiny changes in fundamental forces.
• [Issue] The thorium nucleus's low transition energy arises because strong nuclear and electromagnetic forces nearly cancel, making the clock highly sensitive to changes in fundamental constants.
• [Counterpoint] The prototypes are not yet as precise as the best atomic clocks, though their architecture is proven and upgrades to laser power and crystals are expected to surpass them.
• [Way forward] India should fund optical and nuclear clock research in national metrology laboratories to support navigation systems such as NavIC and secure timing infrastructure.

CA Topic / Headline: The Hindu FAQ on the 2026 Physics Nobel to Francis Halzen: IceCube's 5,160 optical sensors on 86 cables lie 1.4-2.4 km deep in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice; about a hundred of the lakh-odd neutrinos it logs yearly come from astrophysical sources.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• IceCube took full shape in 2011 after seven years of construction; sensors were lowered into holes melted with jets of hot water.
• Cherenkov radiation is the dull blue glow emitted when charged particles move faster than light can in the ice; the sensors record it.
• In 2013 IceCube identified two neutrinos with about 140 times the energy of a proton accelerated by the LHC; in 2017 it traced one to a blazar; in 2022 it found NGC 1068 emitting more neutrinos than expected.
• Halzen and John G. Learned proposed the concept in 1987-88; the project was funded primarily by the U.S. National Science Foundation.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Neutrinos carry no charge, have tiny mass and travel straight, so they reveal sources of cosmic rays that magnetic fields would otherwise hide.
• [Issue] Neutrinos interact rarely with matter, so detection needs enormous detector volume; only around a hundred of the lakh-odd yearly events come from outer space.
• [Way forward] Combining neutrino data with other telescopes can reveal sources of the universe's most energetic particles, a priority for multi-messenger astronomy.
• [Counterpoint] Large detectors are expensive and decades-long; the award committee credited Halzen mainly for keeping hundreds of scientists and engineers working on it for decades.

CA Topic / Headline: The Hindu FAQ on the 2026 Chemistry Nobel to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai: Kagan showed a catalyst's product can be purer than its ingredients; Soai's reaction amplified a 0.00005% handedness excess to over 99.5% in three rounds, supporting Frank's 1953 homochirality model.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Chirality is the property of an object or molecule being non-superimposable on its mirror image; the two mirror forms are called enantiomers.
• Every amino acid in protein is the 'left' (L) form and every sugar in DNA is the 'right' (D) form.
• Thalidomide, a sedative, left thousands of children with birth defects in the early 1960s; ethambutol's (S,S) form is about 500 times more potent against the tuberculosis bacillus than the (R,R) form.
• Charles Frank's 1953 model needed autocatalysis, enantioselective catalysis and an anti-catalyst; asymmetric catalysis had earned Nobel Prizes in 2001 and 2021.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Intro data] Kagan's catalyst with 75% right-handed and 25% left-handed ingredients gave roughly 90:10 product, overturning the assumption that product purity cannot exceed that of the catalyst.
• [Issue] Drug action depends on handedness; the wrong enantiomer can be harmless at best and harmful at worst, so manufacturing pure enantiomers is a pharmaceutical challenge.
• [Counterpoint] The Nobel Committee itself calls Soai's reaction a 'proof of concept' since it uses zinc reagents in organic solvents, nothing like the watery prebiotic soup.
• [Way forward] Asymmetric catalysis can lower dosages and side effects by producing purer drug forms, a gap India's pharmaceutical sector can fill through process research.

CA Topic / Headline: The Hindu FAQ on the 2026 Medicine Nobel to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel: optogenetics uses viral vectors to put light-sensitive opsins such as channelrhodopsin into target neurons, then light pulses switch cells on or off, revealing circuits behind memory, mood and behaviour.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):

• Optogenetics fuses genetic targeting and optical control; the word first appeared in print in late 2006, and Deisseroth published his breakthrough in 2005.
• The prize of 12 million Swedish kronor is shared equally by Deisseroth (Stanford), Hegemann (Humboldt University) and Nagel (University of Würzburg).
• Researchers use harmless viral vectors to deliver opsin genes, then fibre-optic cables or LEDs to activate or silence cells.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):

• [Issue] Researchers use the method on circuits linked to Alzheimer's, dementia, addiction and depression, and in attempts to restore sight; clinical translation remains early.
• [Counterpoint] Delivering genes into brain cells with viral vectors carries safety and ethical questions, and lab findings in mice may not transfer easily to humans.
• [Way forward] Nations must ensure that cutting-edge research reaches the field quickly and benefits all citizens, including older people with neurological conditions.

CA Topic / Headline: SC Special Bench (Justices Joymalya Bagchi, V. Mohana) holds an 'extraordinary' Sunday hearing, directs Centre and Delhi Police to stop illegal detentions, review barricades, keep Internet, Metro and rail running and lift Section 163 BNSS orders around courts, "subject to law and public order".
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• No detention except by law outside the four-km prohibitory zone of central Delhi, which includes Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site; people may assemble peacefully outside the restricted zone.
• Notices issued to Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and DMRC chairperson D. Thara on a contempt plea over the October 9 order barring 'outright prohibition' of Metro and public transport.
• Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta: entry and exit restricted at 45 of 303 Delhi Metro stations; Internet restored. Over 2,500 people were taken into custody on Saturday (Oct 10).
• Himat Lal K. Shah v Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad (1972, Constitution Bench): State can only regulate assembly and impose reasonable restrictions; Anita Thakur v Govt of J&K (2016): peaceful demonstration is a fundamental right.
• Section 163 of the BNSS replaced Section 144 CrPC; Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India (2018) and the Ramlila Maidan case (2012) recognised peaceful protest as a fundamental right.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Judgment] Art 19(1)(a)-(b) with 19(2)-(3): the Bench balanced free movement, access to courts and connectivity against the State's power of reasonable restriction for public order.
• [Issue] Blanket prohibitory orders, Metro closures and mass preventive detentions convert regulation into prohibition; Section 163 is used as a standing tool, and Jantar Mantar reportedly needs applications 10 days ahead.
• [Counterpoint] Police cite non-cooperation by protesters and law-and-order intelligence; courts have upheld designated protest sites and reasonable time-place-manner limits (MKSS 2018).
• [Way forward] Narrow, time-bound, reasoned orders under Section 163; published protest guidelines; name tags and arrest memos per D.K. Basu norms; judicial review of preventive detentions.

CA Topic / Headline: The Hindu recalls Gandhi's March 18, 1922 sedition trial before Ahmedabad Sessions judge C.N. Broomfield over three Young India articles, where he pleaded guilty with editor Shankarlal Banker and defended 'disaffection' without violence, as protesters court detention in Delhi.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Gandhi was tried in 1922 for publishing three articles in his journal Young India; he and editor Shankarlal Ghelabhai Banker pleaded guilty.
• Judge C.N. Broomfield of the Ahmedabad District and Sessions court allowed Gandhi to make a statement in open court; Gandhi said 'affection cannot be manufactured or regulated by law'.
• Gandhi rejected 'violent non-co-operation', which he said only multiplied evil; non-violence implied voluntary submission to the penalty for non-co-operation.
• The trial followed the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922), after which Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement; the charge was under Section 124A IPC (sedition).
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Gandhi's court statement framed civil disobedience as open, non-violent acceptance of legal penalty, the moral template for later satyagrahas.
• [Judgment] Post-Independence, Article 19 constitutionalised that dissent; Kedar Nath Singh (1962) read sedition down to incitement to violence, and S.G. Vombatkere (2022) kept Section 124A in abeyance.
• [Counterpoint] Gandhi accepted punishment willingly; modern protest movements that seek to avoid legal consequences differ from his idea of civil resistance.
• [Intro data] Gandhi called Section 124A the 'prince among the political sections' of the IPC designed to suppress liberty.

Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Form 7 seeks deletion of names; daily Form 7 receipts in each Assembly constituency should be consolidated into Form 10 and uploaded for public scrutiny.
• CEO figures: 67,307 Form 7s (June 16-Aug 23) vs 6,951 on portal; 34,631 (June 16-Sept 9) and 41,792 (June 16-Sept 17) in later releases; 1,10,654 by Oct 8.
• Draft SIR rolls were released on August 24, 2026; the CEO said the claims-and-objections period ran from August 24 to September 23.
• The August 24 statement promised lists of claims and objections in Forms 9, 10, 11, 11A and 11B on the CEO Karnataka website.
• Union Minister Ramdas Athawale claimed 6 crore of the 13 crore SIR deletions were due to changes of residence.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Unpublished deletion forms deny electors notice and the chance to object, weakening the audit trail that guards against wrongful exclusion.
• [Intro data] A false positive (type I error) in roll revision removes an eligible voter; a false negative (type II) keeps an ineligible name; both shrink with more data, appeals and independent audits.
• [Counterpoint] The CEO says counts should cover only the August 24-September 23 window; staggered uploads may reflect workload rather than concealment.
• [Way forward] Real-time booth-wise Form 7 and Form 10 publication, reconciled CEO and ECI data, statutory notice before deletion and third-party audits.

GS Area: GS2 Polity – Election Commission, Constitutional Bodies
CA Topic / Headline: Op-eds by ex-ECI DG Akshay Rout and Mehbooba Mufti question ECI credibility over SIR, the 2023 appointment law and internal dissent by ECs Sandhu and Joshi; IAS officer Prakash Rajpurohit appointed Deputy Election Commissioner after Sanjay Kumar's repatriation.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• The 2023 Act on appointment of Election Commissioners removed the CJI from the selection panel and gives ECs lifelong protection from civil and criminal prosecution for official acts.
• A three-member Commission replaced the single CEC in 1993; Sukumar Sen was CEC for India's first general election (1951); the ECI runs IIIDEM to train election managers abroad.
• About 98 crore electors were on the rolls for the 2024 Lok Sabha election; the SIR excluded over 13 crore names from draft rolls.
• Prakash Rajpurohit (2010-batch, Rajasthan cadre) appointed DEC by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet till April 8, 2030; predecessor Sanjay Kumar signed the June 24, 2025 order initiating the SIR.
• Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls and elections in the ECI; a CEC can be removed only like an SC judge.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Trust, not logistics, is now the ECI's deficit: Rout contrasts Sukumar Sen's logistical challenges in 1951 with today's crisis of credibility.
• [Committee] Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) and Anoop Baranwal v Union of India (2023) favoured a neutral selection panel including the CJI or LoP.
• [Counterpoint] Supporters say executive-led appointment is constitutionally valid under Article 324(2) and that SIR cleans rolls of migrants and the dead.
• [Way forward] Collegium-style appointment, statutory security of tenure for ECs, recorded dissent, and transparent work allocation for DECs handling rolls and IT.

Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• Economic Survey 2026 estimates the strain of unconditional cash transfers on States at ₹1.7 lakh crore.
• Anti-defection provisions are in the Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985); the 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the one-third 'split' exception, leaving the two-thirds merger exception (para 4).
• Disqualification petitions are decided by the Speaker/Chairman; Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld the Schedule and made the decision subject to judicial review.
• Speaker's recognition of factions and ECI's symbol allocation under the Symbols Order, 1968 are the follow-up decisions after a mass defection.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Issue] Pre-poll cash transfers labelled welfare and post-poll wholesale defections both distort the voter's mandate and the level playing field.
• [Judgment] Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) asked Speakers to decide disqualification petitions within three months; S. Subramaniam Balaji (2013) asked ECI to frame freebie guidelines.
• [Way forward] Rout's agenda: regulate political finance and freebies, decriminalise politics, counter AI-abetted fake narratives, and an all-party compact to fortify elections.
• [Counterpoint] Cash transfers can be legitimate redistribution; courts have been wary of defining 'freebies', which is a fiscal-policy choice of elected governments.
